title: CNI route suppression leading to scheduler deadlock — playbook WIP
content:
Summary:

This is a working playbook for a recurring failure mode we've observed on a subset of GPU-backed worker pools: the CNI on a node sometimes drops the pod CIDR / local host routes (or the kernel suppresses them), which leads to NodeNetworkUnavailable predicates for the kube-scheduler, causing a scheduling 'deadlock' where pods remain Pending even though nodes show Ready. The behaviour is intermittent and often correlates with high network offload activity, NIC firmware/driver updates, or kernel XDP/ethtool offload changes.

Why this doc exists (notes to self):
- We keep re-triaging similar incidents (SRE-4821, SRE-3910) and the checklist/diagnostics are slightly different from standard cni-restart playbooks.
- Need a compact detection + mitigation flow for on-call that avoids mass reboots.

Observed symptoms (typical):
- New pods in GPU pools stay Pending with message: "0/12 nodes are available: 6 node(s) had taints that the pod didn't tolerate, 6 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict, 12 node(s) were not ready" or generic "no nodes are available" even though nodes show Ready in kubectl.
- kube-scheduler logs show repeated rejections with predicate NodeNetworkUnavailable or NodeNotReady-like checks.
- Affected nodes respond slowly to liveness/readiness checks; kubelet node_status_update_duration spikes.
- Network debugging from node shows missing pod CIDR routes (pod CIDR not present in ip route table), or iptables MASQUERADE rules missing for pod CIDR.
- CNI plugin logs (on the node /var/log/containers, /var/log/host/containernetworking/*) show spurious failures applying route changes or netlink errors (e.g., "RTM_SETROUTE: file exists" / "no such process").

First-response checklist (fast path - <20min):
1) Confirm scope
   - kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o wide | grep Pending
   - kubectl get nodes -l pool=gpu -o wide
   - Identify candidate nodes with many pending scheduled pods: inspect pod spec's nodeSelector/affinity to pick nodes likely targeted.

2) Quick node-level checks (run on suspected node via ssh or through bastion):
   - ip route show table main | grep <pod-cidr>    # look for pod CIDR routes
   - iptables -t nat -S | grep <pod-cidr>        # check MASQ rules for pod CIDR
   - journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager | tail -n 100  # any recent network errors
   - ls /var/log/containernetworking || ls /var/log/cni           # CNI logs
   - ps aux | grep kube-proxy; check kube-proxy logs for conntrack errors

3) Confirm scheduler predicate failure
   - kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/kube-scheduler -c kube-scheduler --since=10m | grep NodeNetworkUnavailable || grep "predicate"
   - If scheduler reports NodeNetworkUnavailable for that node, proceed.

Short-term mitigations (aim to restore scheduling quickly):
Option A: Repair CNI without node reboot (preferred)
   - kubectl -n kube-system get daemonset <cni-daemonset> -o name
   - kubectl -n kube-system exec -it ds/<cni-daemonset> -c <cni-container> -- sh -c "ls /host/var/run/netns || true"
   - Restart the CNI plugin process where available: kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart daemonset/<cni-daemonset> --if-exists
   - On node: sudo systemctl restart <cni-agent-service> or restart the container runtime's pause infra for quick netns re-population.

Option B: Evacuate / restart kube-proxy on affected node
   - ssh node; sudo systemctl restart kube-proxy OR kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l k8s-app=kube-proxy --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
   - This often restores conntrack / iptables setup without touching CNI in some cases.

Option C: Cordon + drain (if repairs fail)
   - kubectl cordon <node>
   - kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
   - If drain hangs due to stuck kubelet, consider force-reboot of node (last resort).

Quick diagnostics to capture during incident (copy/paste to ticket):
- kubectl describe node <node>  # conditions, taints, kubelet version
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 500 --no-pager | sed -n '1,200p'
- sudo ip route show table main
- sudo iptables -t nat -S | head -n 200
- ls -l /var/run/netns
- ps -ef | grep aws-node || true   # or cni binary name
- cat /etc/cni/net.d/10-aws.conflist || cat /etc/cni/net.d/*
- docker/containerd: sudo crictl ps -a --namespace=k8s.io
- kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide

Root-cause hypothesis (working list):
- Race between CNI modifications and NIC driver offload causing kernel-level route suppression (some NICs implement suppression/XDP that removes routes until re-asserted).
- conntrack/skewed iptables state when kube-proxy or CNI restarts under load; kube-scheduler sees NodeNetworkUnavailable because NodeStatus conditions lag behind real network repairs.
- A particular CNI version (v1.3.8 in our fleet) has a regression where it skips re-creating a local route when MTU offload fails.

Longer-term mitigations (engineering backlog):
- Upgrade CNI plugin to v1.4.x which contains netlink retry/backoff fix (see PR #87).
- Add a node-level watchdog that periodically asserts pod CIDR routes exist and, if missing, triggers local CNI reapply and alerts SRE.
- Add a kubelet/kube-proxy readiness probe that triggers earlier recovery actions when iptables rules are inconsistent.
- Work with infra to update NIC firmware/drivers on gpu node image and disable aggressive XDP offload toggles.

Prometheus and alerting suggestions (to add to prod rules):
- Alert: node_podcidr_missing (expression: count by(node) (absent(kubelet_node_spec_pod_cidr{node="$node"})) > 0 for 5m)
- Alert: node_network_unavailable_count (increase if more than 2 nodes show NodeNetworkUnavailable for >3m)
- Dashboards: pending_pods_by_pool, kubelet_node_status_update_latency, cni_restart_rate

Playbook escalation matrix (who to call):
- SRE on-call (primary) — run first-response checklist
- CNI owner (networking team) — if restarts didn't fix within 20 minutes, assign to Diego
- Infra (image/kernel) — if NIC firmware suspected, loop in Priya

Open questions / follow-ups (todo):
- Confirm exact kernel version(s) that exhibit route suppression under test in gpu-pool image 2025-10-12.
- Build a synthetic load test that toggles large numbers of netlink updates to reproduce quickly in staging.
- Decide whether kube-scheduler should treat NodeNetworkUnavailable as transitory for nodes with Ready==True for short windows (RFC?).

Incident notes template (cut+paste into JIRA):
- Impact: pods Pending in gpu pool for X minutes; automation pipelines delayed; no data plane loss for existing pods.
- Scope: N nodes affected across AZs A and C; repeating since 2026-01-02.
- Mitigation taken: restarts of CNI ds on affected nodes, kube-proxy restart, cordon/drain of 3 nodes, full node reboots for 2 nodes.
- Root-cause hypothesis: race between CNI and NIC driver offload (see linked PR).
- Follow-ups: upgrade CNI, firmware update, add pod-cidr watchdog.

Notes to on-call: keep this doc open when triaging. If you make a procedural change during an incident (commands, additional checks), paste it into the ticket and update this doc so we can bake into runbook.

Appendix: Useful commands (copyable)
- Find example affected nodes: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.status.phase=="Pending") | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, nodes: .spec.nodeName, message: .status.conditions?}'
- Check routes on node: sudo ip route show table main | grep $(cat /var/lib/kubelet/pod-resources/kubelet.log 2>/dev/null || echo <pod-cidr>)
- Reapply CNI config (node): sudo systemctl restart cni || sudo docker restart $(docker ps -q --filter name=cni-plugin)
- Force kube-proxy pod restart: kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l k8s-app=kube-proxy --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>

-- end of draft --
